sentences.text: This bird featured a long beak that curved downwards, paired with greatly reduced wings and robust legs ending in elongate toes.
Forbes estimated the animal measured 40 cm in length and weighed 2 kg, noting its short leg bones indicated complete flightlessness.
Henry Ogg Forbes described the species in 1892 after receiving fossil bones, including a distinctive skull, from William Hawkins.
Due to the strength of its beak, it is suggested the bird could consume a wide variety of prey, including ground-dwelling petrel chicks.
Researchers suggest the bird may have finally gone extinct in the early European era due to introduced non-native mammals like cats, dogs, rats, and pigs.
Forbes later moved the species to the separate genus Diaphorapteryx in 1892 but eventually reverted to placing it in Aphanapteryx.
Charles William Andrews criticized the close relationship between the two rails in 1896, while Hans Friedrich Gadow suggested their similar morphology resulted from parallel evolution.
The species was endemic to the Chatham Islands east of New Zealand, specifically found on Chatham Island and Pitt Island.
The species lived during the Holocene, from approximately 0.0117 million years ago until 0 million years ago.
It is debated whether the bird went extinct between 1550 and 1700 AD or much later, based on conflicting European assumptions and Moriori oral histories.
